subject: Large Standard Errors around Occupancy Coefficient Estimates

messages.author: 699590c68f803362
messages.subject: Large Standard Errors around Occupancy Coefficient Estimates
parts:
Hello, 

I am running single season occupancy models for a secretive marsh bird.  I sampled at 50 sites 5 times each.  I am currently running occupancy models in unmarked to gain information about the relationship between this species and its habitat.  Below is my detection history distribution:

00000 - 41 sites
10000 - 3 sites
01000 - 3 sites
00100 - 1 site
00010 - 1 site
01001 - 1 site  

Almost all of my models come out with huge standard error estimates for the occupancy covariates (I have included 2 examples of model outputs below).  I've run goodness of fit tests and bootstrapping on the models, as well as getting AUC scores, and they show really good model fit, but I am very concerned about the standard errors.

> summary(km10a)
Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ Emergent_2km + OpenWater_2km, data = umf, 
    control = list(maxit = 10000))

Occupancy (logit-scale):
                        Estimate    SE      z        P(>|z|)
(Intercept)              -59.5  92.9 -0.640   0.522
Emergent_2km     107.4 166.4  0.646   0.518
OpenWater_2km    -40.4  65.7 -0.615   0.538

Detection (logit-scale):
 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
    -2.92 0.325 -8.98 2.69e-19

AIC: 87.00038 
Number of sites: 50
optim convergence code: 0
optim iterations: 539 
Bootstrap iterations: 0

> summary(c8b)

Call:
occu(formula = ~length ~ MAWR + SORA + Emergent_2km + WetForest_2km + 
    Forest_2km, data = umf, control = list(maxit = 10000))

Occupancy (logit-scale):
                      Estimate  SE      z        P(>|z|)
(Intercept)             -309 426 -0.724   0.469
MAWR                   159 181  0.877   0.380
SORA                    -184 223 -0.825   0.409
Emergent_2km       223 287  0.775   0.438
WetForest_2km     -264 320 -0.825   0.409
Forest_2km            242 391  0.618   0.536

Detection (logit-scale):
            Estimate   SE     z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -3.71 1.80 -2.06  0.0396
length          2.13 1.82  1.17  0.2416

AIC: 70.35539 
Number of sites: 50
optim convergence code: 0
optim iterations: 459 
Bootstrap iterations: 0

Are these large standard errors due to the fact that I only have one site with a repeat detection?  If so, would collapsing the detection history and using logistic modeling instead be a good choice?  Is there something else that can cause these large standard errors to occur?  I appreciate any advice anyone has on this issue!

Thank you, 

Michelle Kane

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Large Standard Errors around Occupancy Coefficient Estimates
parts:
I think the problem is that the models you're trying to fit are far too complex for the available data.  There are only 9 sites with detections and just 10 detections.  Not only are the standard errors large but the estimated coefficients are also large enough to cause concern.

I assume (maybe incorrectly) that Emergent_2km and OpenWater_2km take on values 0 and 1.  If you construct the occupancy estimates for all 4 combinations, you'll get occupancy probabilities of 0 and 1.

Jim

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Large Standard Errors around Occupancy Coefficient Estimates
parts:
Here's an attempt (well, with a bit of hand waving) to answer your question about collapsing the detection history and using logistic modeling.

If we condition on just the sites with at least one detection, then you have 10 detections over 45 visits.  Using 10/45 = 0.22222 likely gives you an over-estimate of the probability of detection for a single visit.  For 5 visits we would then expect a probability of 1 - (1 - 10/45)^5 = 0.715 to obtain at least 1 detection.

For me, 0.715 is just too low to switch to logistic regression.  Using your first model has the estimate of the per visit detection probability at 0.051 which results in 1-(1-0.051)^5 = 0.23 for the probability of at least one detection which is even lower.

So, in short, I don't think you should switch to logistic regression.

Jim
